title: Health and disease in hot climates
sentences: My Curators, Professors, Doctors, Students, and all of you who take an interest in Higher Education in this place,
highly esteemed Hearers!
Although the time still seems far off when hygiene—as some would have it—will already be taught in primary school,
the great value of health is nevertheless imprinted upon us all from our youth.
That health is the greatest treasure, and that a sound mind can properly dwell only in a sound body—there you have what
that have been repeatedly presented to us, now in the dress of this then again in the garb of that ancient or modern language.
So repeatedly, that doubt about its general validity,
which, with regard to the latter statement, at least does not seem to be devoid of all grounds, hardly occurs to us.
Less irrefutable, however, is the traditional conception of the learned and unlearned pedagogues, as if health were the attribute of poverty,
illness, on the other hand, are the almost inseparable companion of wealth: the needy, but healthy and satisfied daily wage earner,
the pleasurable and opulent, but grumpy and sickly richness are standing types from the stories of our youth.
Now there may be, also in a literal sense, a lot of truth in the saying that they are strong legs,
who carry the wealth, who from the other side would be in our zoo
socialist times still dare to doubt, when the statistician calculates us in advance,
that it is poverty in the highest degree that makes health and life chances so much worse?
Even there have been those who saw in the greater mortality among the less fortunate the expression of an inexorable law of nature,
the self-regulation of population density in connection with the limited resources of the community;
a necessary evil, against which even hygienic measures would in the long run be powerless.
And even if that performance was one-sided and exaggerated, it certainly is,
that the matter of public health is closely related to public welfare not only in the sense that 'commonhealth is commonwealth', but above all vice versa,
so that general physical prosperity is a prerequisite for cultivating a healthy and powerful people.
Hence, those discoveries in the field of science and industry and those reforms of a socio-economic nature,
which bring the most necessary necessities of life more within the reach of the lower classes,
certainly benefit public health no less than discoveries of a purely hygienic nature.
Because, as far as the latter is concerned, one can point to a success like that of cowpox vaccination,
but this has not yet been matched by any similar.
On the other hand, with consistent application, the prescriptions of health science can intervene in personal and community life to such an extent,
that the charity is surpassed.
The physician must therefore understand that he is also minister non magister naturae in the field of hygiene and that he must not lose sight of the 'primum est medici ne noceat' here either.
Certainly, the physician-hygienist is above all human and considers nothing human strange; as a child of his
time, he participates according to his aptitude and temperament in
the questions of the day and is involved in the political and social currents.
Where study and work gave him above many the opportunity to increase his knowledge,
to broaden his view, he undoubtedly has the right, yes it is his duty,
to maintain his position as a citizen and to assert his voice outside his actual territory.
But first and foremost, the voice of the citizen, not that of the skilled person.
Even on issues of close concern to public health, if there are those of alcohol abuse, prostitution, vegetarianism,
the fight against epidemics, colonisation and tutti quanti issues, which can be viewed from so different sides,
where religion and morality, customs and tradition, race and climate, politics and economics, science and technology exert their influence as a struggle,
there, he would not be the expert in excellence, to whom the final decision must be left.
His task is more modest, thus gaining in depth, which she loses in breadth.
The practitioner of health science must face society as the forensic physician faces the judge.
He has to answer the questions he has in his special field by
the community and to prepare for this through study and through own research in and outside the workplaces of his science.
This is the point of view on which I believe he, too, should position himself,
who is called to the dual task of teaching health science and contributing to the increase of that branch of science.

'About health and illness in hot regions.'
Between the tropics, the fertile regions are unhealthy, the healthy regions are infertile, so it is not entirely wrong to complain.
Indeed, the cooperation of high temperature and humidity in the tropical beach climate is,
that not only creates lush plant growth,
but also gives rise to numerous visible and invisible living germs and, in addition, directly exerts its exhausting and debilitating influence on humans.
Nevertheless, the aforementioned complaint is not entirely fair.
After all, it is based on an overly particularistic point of view, the personal interests and experiences of the white person, the foreigner,
in the foreground, ignoring the fact that these same unhealthy countries nevertheless harbour a flourishing indigenous population almost everywhere.
But in addition, compared to the past, a significant improvement in the general state of health is also noticeable among the European population of the tropic countries,
although it is difficult to put under figures everywhere.
The progress in all kinds of areas, the living conditions that have improved so much over time,
who have made such a powerful contribution to raising public health in Europe, have reduced mortality so significantly,
have also not been without influence on the physical well-being of the tropical inhabitants.
Since it is no longer the scum of European society,
from which the immigrants recruit themselves, have brought about a complete reversal in the conditions of existence since the improved means of transport
and through the greater contact with the motherland, the greater influx of civilized women, the mores became so much softer,
the immoderation and recklessness have been so much tempered, since more and more good medical care and the application of sanitary measures are taken care of,
the proverbial unhealthiness of the tropical climate has already lost many of its horrors.
No wonder that the pessimistic judgments of yesteryear have changed significantly in favor,
yes, already have to make way for somewhat overly optimistic performances.
'Malaria, yellow fever, dysentery, liver abscess, beri-beri and cholera, the scourges of the tropics, are all - one argues - preventable diseases.
Avoidable, because newer science has revealed its causes and thus
has put in place the means to combat them successfully.
Now, take away those diseases and causes of disease and you have: the sent tropical inhabitant, the 'permanent summer man.'
If finger-pointing to a distant appears, and that is how it will also be intended, this prediction certainly has its value;
to take her in full seriousness now could be and know his overestimation of us at present.
It is true, in order to successfully combat an ailment, it is of the utmost importance,
yes, it is indispensable to know its causes.
And in this respect, with regard to infectious diseases, we have the latest batch of experimental science,
bacteriology or, more correctly, microbiology, is already much to be thanked for.
But with finding the microbes and studying their action on the organism,
people are not yet getting to know those causes of disease from all sides.
After all, it is the task of hygiene
to investigate the pathogenic microbes, especially in their occurrence and their living conditions outside the living body.
So first she will learn to fully understand and explain the epidemiological phenomena,
and on that basis perhaps - because even this does not speak for itself - can indicate rational pesticides.
As far as all that is concerned, we have no reason to boast too much about the triumphs of our science.
That the malaria parasites also find the conditions for their development in the outside world,
is not subject to any reasonable doubt, nevertheless, no one has yet succeeded in finding them there with certainty.
So far, their presence has only been demonstrated in the blood of malaria sufferers.
With Asian cholera, we are a bit further in that respect,
but still - whatever one may say in this regard - far from where we should be.
I would like to recall how Robert Koch expressed his positive opinion about the specificity of the bacilli he discovered.
the dejections of cholera sufferers discovered kommabacil was mainly based on this coincidence: a sharply characterized by morphological and biological properties,
and from other easily distinguishable microbes, constantly and exclusively occurring in, and in connection with the said disease.
What was brought to light in the first years after this discovery by him and others in this field,
only helped to substantiate Koch 's statement.
While on the one hand by researchers in all parts of the world again and again
the presence of the Kommabacil in cholera could be demonstrated and contradictory findings appeared to be based on error,
it seemed, on the other hand, that his Kommabacil was nowhere to be found without the disease.
Regarding the last point, Koch did not find it difficult at first
those few cases, in which curved microbes were found unrelated to cholera and considered by their discoverers to be identical with his,
to demonstrate the inaccuracy of that opinion.
Furthermore, until a few years ago, it could be argued against the Kommabacil as a specific cause of disease with some justification that it,
against fair expectation, only in a few rare cases had the comabacilli in the prevailing cholera
tracing the outside world - this gap has also been filled since then, thanks to the improved and sharpened methods of research.
Nevertheless, the problem has not become any easier with it, on the contrary.
Because not only have cholera microbes now also been found in apparently healthy people,
but in addition, doppelgangers have been found in cholera-free times, which are hardly distinguishable from them.
And this is all the more important because it has been shown from the other side,
that Koch 's Kommabacil in its characteristics indicated as characteristic does not offer that constancy everywhere and at all times,
if, in the past and to a certain extent, it is still attributed to this and can be considered of such great importance for a certain diagnosis.
With that variability, with the fluctuations in virulence, among other things
of the pathogenic microbes, so important from an epidemiological point of view, experimental science took little or no account in the beginning.
The German school in particular, at the risk of being guilty of petitio principii,
the limits of the concept of species in bacteriology.
Meanwhile, that doctrinairism, born at a time,
when people were still forming the most fantastic ideas about the chaos of microorganisms, their origin, meaning and changeable properties, outside
doubt also had its good side.
In any case, it had a great didactic and heuristic value and in
the fruits of that, after all, it also finds its own corrective.
Because the more knowledge, the less scholarship.
So there is in this area - who will deny it,
but who else will avenge it in such a young science?
- so there is a lot of à refaire.
Many a fact, which already seemed to have been established for good, has again been put into question, by many a prescribed measure,
that previously seemed rational, but now when the unripe fruit of half-knowledge shows itself, the usefulness has become very problematic.
But even when the chaff is separated from the wheat,
we will have reason to be satisfied with the harvest.
And there are plenty of bright spots in the future.
I would like to point out here in the first place the increasingly prominent striving to prevent diseases not by
keep the causes of the disease away from the body, but by increasing the resistance of the organism,
a goal that promises to bear such beautiful fruit in the field of infectious diseases as well.
Attempts to create artificial immunity where natural incompatibility is lacking or inadequate,
similar to those in India by Haffkine in the case of cholera and plague, by Sanarelli in Brazil in the case of yellow fever.
Attempts, which find their prototype in the cowpox vaccination, but whose rational and versatile application is first of all due to the discoveries of Pasteur,
Koch, Behring, Pfeiffer and other microbiologists.
Of a completely different nature are the remedies that have been at our service for many years against the so pernicious malaria.
Dehydration of the soil as a contraceptive, kina as a medicine, we owe them to empathy and the
instinct of the indigenous peoples.
Nevertheless, here too, the help of the miscroop is of the greatest importance, both in view of the timely and certain recognition of the disease,
as to indicate the correct time, at which therapeutic intervention is most likely to be successful.
Or insects, which undoubtedly act as carriers of the contaminant in many infectious diseases, also play such a role in malaria and or
so the fight against that disease will end in a fight against the mosquitoes, the future must learn.
Is it on the west coast of tropical Africa the deadly sleeping sickness that threatens the native, while sparing the white,
elsewhere - so in our East Indian colonies - it is the beri-beri, who, albeit less exclusively, take over that role.
Will science and experience, hand in hand, soon succeed in eradicating this cancer from our colonial existence?
The omens seem favorable.
Dysentery, which used to occur so severely and frequently in our colonies because of its dreaded disease,
takes a much more modest place on our morbidity and mortality lists today - with the exception of passers-by and purely local ones.
Provide good drinking water, a more hygienic lifestyle has probably contributed a lot to this.
Points of light over so - I repeat - that we,
albeit here and there only from a distance, counter-rays, clear enough, however, to make you see,
that the beautiful premonitions, to which I referred at that time, are still something more than the product of a vivid imagination.
But with the re-closing of Pandora's box, not everything would have been won.
Health is not only a negation of illness, it is also based on a more positive understanding.
Full access to mental and physical functions, a resilient constitution, a spacious
degree of physical pleasure, that is what stamps the sent person.
Much of it must be lacking for the white tropical inhabitant.
The consolation that he is a permanent summer person cannot - however well-intentioned - compensate him for that lack.
As anemic and powerless people, only recovered from a serious, exhausting illness,
for example, show themselves to the eye of the newly arrived white people, who have already been in the tropics for some time.
But even he himself, although he is spared from illness, loses the blushing facial color in a few months, becomes slow in his movements,
seeks body rest at the hottest hours of the day, while the domestic element is in full swing around him.
In the absence of sufficient tools for physiological research, people used to make this more or less a priori idea of the changes,
grasp that place in the body of the resident of cooler regions, when he has been transferred in the hot climate.
His former environment - so they reasoned - and his aptitude and organisation developed in connection with it brought with it,
that his metabolism and heat production, his strength development was lively, his skin activity was low.
With its displacement into the greenhouse atmosphere of the tropics, there must be a complete turnaround in that organization, in those transactions.
In other words: his body must undergo an acclimatization process if he wants to eventually ground in the zoo's changed environment.
Do we already see that, in order to find a debouché for the accumulated body heat, his skin activity increases significantly,
the sweat secretion has increased until it becomes superfluous, gradually his body focuses sustainably on it, so as to reduce
possible to generate heat.
Not only that the muscular activity, that source of mechanical force but also of heat, is limited to the bare minimum,
that, partly due to the lack of the stimulating stimulus of the cold, the metabolism becomes less powerful, the need for food decreases,
not only that the breaths decrease in depth and supply less oxygen to the blood due to the greater thinness of the hot air,
but also the composition of the blood changes in harmony with it; the blood becomes thinner and paler.
This was the meaning of the anemia and of the less powerful expressions of life of the European tropical inhabitant.
They allow him to better tolerate the heat,
not by increasing his active resistance, but by a passive compliance with it.
Thus, according to the train of thought shown here, the acclimated white man is a weakling, who leads a languishing existence,
an inferior one, whose state of health is in unstable equilibrium with the many pathogenic influences to which he has been exposed in the tropics.
What a contrast to the native!
His pigmented skin surpasses, as is commonly imagined, the fair skin in its ability to radiate the excess body heat,
that neither an excessive, but at the same time so debilitating sweat secretion,
nor a significant reduction in the heat-generating life processes need to be aided in order to preserve the heat balance.
With him, therefore, no anemia, no significantly reduced life energy, no increased susceptibility to pathogenic influences.
So much for theory.
It must be acknowledged that,
since physiological deduction has given way to experimental research in this area,
our ideas about the influence of heat on the constitution of the tropical inhabitant have had to change not insignificantly.
there is no such thing as physiological anemia in hot countries.
The blood of the white tropical inhabitant is no paler
and richer in water than that of the native or that of his conspecifics in cooler regions.
The morbidly appearing paleness of his face is a local phenomenon, due to lesser filling of the skin vessels, not an expression of general anemia.
It is probably in line with the paleness, generally characteristic of those parts of the body,
which are covered by clothing, are, so to speak, in the long run in an artificially humid and warm climate.
It is no different with the native of the tropical regions.
He, too, is pale in the heat and acquires a flushing facial colour when he stays in the cool for a long time;
but the difference is less noticeable with him than with the white because of the covering pigment layer of the epidermis.
Also the assumption that, apart from the influence of muscle activity on metabolism and heat production, the latter operations,
in the case of the white tropical inhabitant, would fall to a lower level, has not proved true on closer examination.
In the state of rest and moderate work, the dust consumption and consequently also the heat production is not greater in the native than in the European,
not more significantly in the cool than in the hot climate.
In the meantime, no one will be able to deduce from these results of racial physiology, from these results of exact comparative research, that the earlier representations
entirely to the realm of myths.
Not only are there unmistakable differences, anatomical as well as physiological, between the different races - e.g.
in the structure and function of the skin - but it is to be expected that these differences will acquire even greater significance, yes,
that there are, which will actually only become noticeable when higher demands are made on the bodily functions, on the compensatory operations first and foremost.
Because one must not lose sight of the fact that in this area experimental research,
as that is actually only feasible with the tools of a well-equipped laboratory, has only just begun.
The comparative studies on metabolism and heat production, of which I mentioned earlier,
have only dealt with the state of rest or light work, as is the rule for white tropical dwellers.
What will the results be if the research is extended to the condition of heavier and, above all, of longer-term work?
If the work performance is the same, the heat production will not be greater, the heat emission will not be more difficult,
in short, the heat control does not turn out to be more insufficient for the white than for the native?
Will the fatigue, the exhaustion at last, not occur earlier in the first than in the last?
It would be premature to want to give a definite answer to those questions right now.
Wanting to decree racial equality also with regard to the climate on the basis of anthropological ideas about
the unit of origin of the human sex is certainly not permissible.
Even if one assumes that unity, it will still remain true,
that what the centuries and the climate have separated cannot immediately be reconciled by a spell of power.
It cannot be denied that the often so windless,
for the feeling of such a lead-heavy atmosphere of the tropics presses much less on the colored native than on the white,
whom she turns persistent mental and physical exertion into a true torment.
It is true, there are examples that Europeans have braved great fatigue on hunting, on military marches in the tropics.
However, we must not overlook the fact that not a few have fallen victim to it,
just as little as such an extraordinary effort was always followed by a long period of rest.
With persistent heavy work even at the hottest hours of the day,
like that with which an agricultural population is concerned, this is not the same.
Precisely in the persistent, the permanent hides, to me, the danger also occurs here.
For the maintenance of normal bodily functions, of health, appropriate alternation of effort and rest is necessary, keeping measure in everything.
The hotter the climate, the higher the demands on the body's heat regulation and the sooner fatigue occurs,
to that extent, muscle work, which after all works in the same direction, is more likely to pose the risk of exceeding physiological limits.
A few times this may not have any adverse consequences, in the long run these will not go away.
Here, too, the 'gutta cavat lapidem' applies.
We don't know what it is that makes the heat so exhausting.
The physiology and pathology of fatigue is still a little developed field.
With the adoption of fatigue substances as products of the metabolism in
the working muscles have not been explained in all cases, not even ours.
After all, the fatigue
the heat is felt immediately in the morning after waking up and is often reduced by light movements.
Also a slightly elevated body temperature, a slight fever in other words
can't be the cause of it.
At the time, this was considered a normal phenomenon for the tropical inhabitant, but this is certainly incorrect.
The physiological blood heat is no greater in the hot countries than in the cool regions.
Anyone who feels tired from the heat therefore does not yet have an elevated body temperature; the test is easy enough to take.
Finally, an altered blood distribution under the influence of the heat stimulus has been thought of,
as a result of which the random muscles would receive too little, the abdominal intestines too much blood.
This would also explain the great tendency to abdominal disorders in the tropics.
I will not elaborate on these issues, however important, in the absence of reliable data.

The state of exhaustion and listlessness has coupled me with psychological irritability, to which the European in the tropics,

that they have been labelled with the name of neurasthenia or nerve exhaustion, although the objective evidence for this exhaustion has not yet been provided.
In this respect, one could therefore speak with more justification than of a tropical anemia of a tropical neurasthenia.
Only one should not imagine it worse than it is.
When no naturally weak nervous system, no physical or mental overstrain, no disease,
no other aggravating circumstances of a social or moral nature have contributed to it, so the phenomena are rather fleeting.
They soon disappear, as soon as a fresher air washes around us again.

It should come as no surprise to us that, in the meantime, with the abundance of the complications mentioned above, many Europeans find themselves forced to seek out cooler regions after several years in order to recover their disturbed nervous life.
It's one of the main reasons,
why a stay in the tropics' sans esprit de retour 'is so difficult for them to achieve.
There is little or no room for our body to actually get used to the tropical heat.
In this respect, I think the much-discussed acclimation consists more in an appearance than in an inner process.
More in making themselves second nature through imitation and habit of a more peculiarly climate-appropriate way of life,
than in appropriate changes to our natural organisation itself.
The austerity in food and drink of the native, his airy clothes, his festina spring, his calm,
resigned philosophy of life therefore deserve, from a purely sanitary point of view, to be set as an example to the white tropical inhabitant.
In the tropical countries, the indigenous population generally feeds mainly on plant-based food,
which is naturally rich in carbohydrates, but relatively poor in proteins and fats.
Whether this is only done out of instinctive fulfillment of the requirements of the climate, however, is not so certain.

too rich a fat diet would lead to digestive disorders.

that when fat is consumed, a relatively larger proportion of the energy accumulated in it is converted into heat than when carbohydrates are consumed.
A view that is more in line with the experience,
that a high-fat diet is more popular in a cold than in a warm climate.

Here, the good intention, unilaterally informed by a preconceived opinion, plays tricks on common sense.
By the way, also in other areas - I think of legislation, education, religion,

is not one of a purely hygienic nature.

that come into play and to which I have already had the opportunity to refer, we disregard and consult the bare experience.
It lasts only three centuries now that movement, that flow of thousands and hundreds of thousands from ancient Europe to the overseas countries,
where Portuguese and Spaniard have shown us the way.
And the result?
Everywhere outside the tropic zone and the countries bordering it, everywhere where summer and winter alternate, in North America, in South Africa, in South Australia,
Tasmania and New Zealand, we see the white race, defying all dangers and objections, gaining a fixed footing, reducing and displacing the native.
How completely different in the hot regions.
Beyond an aristocratic minority, the thoroughbred European gets nowhere.
Where it seems otherwise, as in the lowlands of Mexico, on some West Indies islands, they and their pure descendants, the creoles,

Coloured people, but who have officially undergone a blanchissement due to a complaint from the tax authorities,

Because elsewhere than in the countries mentioned, also in our Indian Archipelago,
coloured people figure in large numbers and even full-blooded natives as Europeans on the registers.

can claim that in the long run the Germans cannot ground in the Dutch climate,

But the fact that the white races dominate everywhere in the temperate air zone in number strength proves,

that the native here can engage in the struggle for existence with the superior white with much more success, that this superiority is therefore only relative.
Yes, where the indigenous population was sparsely sown, workers from elsewhere, negroes, Indian coolies,

lack of protection and cooperation, if not opposition from above are rife.

It seems very likely to me.
Engineering and
industry supported by science stand for nothing, where it applies to man in the struggle to help existence.
If it is not possible to make it suitable for the climate, they make the climate suitable for humans.
After all, the so-called temperate region actually deserves that name first,

created a comfortable artificial environment.
Why should the fight against heat not lead to a similar, albeit more difficult to achieve result?
Cooling indoors and outdoors, considerable relief of the task of the workers through gradually improved tools, accelerated means of transport,
that make the weeks to days, the days to hours, and all that so little precious, that it is generally applicable,

Viewed in this way, the question of colonisation is first and foremost a technical-economic problem, the solution of which is left to time.
Whether that solution is desirable, what fate the native will experience in the process, see here, to which I must remain indebted for the answer.
The zeitgeist cannot be stopped in its progress, hygiene must also be kept up with the flow,
through good information, trying to bring her own to lead it in the desired direction.
Good information requires knowledge, zoomed research, where that knowledge falls short, and teaching, in order to spread that knowledge.
At the high flight that nature research has taken in this century,
it is not surprising that this has also benefited the tropical countries and
has also sought and found a wide field of work there.
Medical and especially hygienic science has amply received its share of this.
Scientific expeditions went out to study cholera and plague in the focal points of infection,

The Netherlands has not lagged behind in its East Indian colonies in terms of this and in general in terms of the promotion of public health.

while a corps of state-trained domestic medicine officials - too small, admittedly, for the needs - devote their concerns to the population,

If so much has already been done, much remains to be done.
